title: FSSAI Licence Suspension Cannot Continue Once Compliance Is Restored, Rules Bombay High Court
meta_description: Bombay HC's Kolhapur Bench holds an FSSAI licence suspension must be revoked once re-inspection shows compliance, rejecting its use as a standing penalty.
bench: Justice Sharmila U. Deshmukh and Justice Neeraj P. Dhote
case_name: Hotel Alankar v. State of Maharashtra
body: An establishment that fixes the problems a food safety inspector flagged should get its licence back, not keep answering for a violation that no longer exists. That, in essence, is what the Bombay High Court's Kolhapur Bench told the State of Maharashtra when a food business authority tried to keep a suspension running well after the hotel it targeted had cleaned up its act.

The sequence of inspections told its own story. A surprise inspection on 7 July 2026 found the hotel's food safety compliance at just 69 per cent, and the licensing authority suspended its licence the very next day under Section 32(3) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, the provision that lets an authority act immediately where public health is at stake. The hotel moved quickly to fix what the inspection had found, and a re-inspection on 31 July recorded 97 per cent compliance, a figure the Division Bench treated as proof that the underlying public health concern had been resolved.

Despite that turnaround, the suspension was kept in place, prompting the hotel to approach the High Court. Justices Sharmila U. Deshmukh and Neeraj P. Dhote framed the question squarely: does Section 32(3) authorise an open-ended suspension, or is it confined to the period during which the public health risk that justified it actually persists? The bench came down firmly on the latter reading.

Suspension under Section 32(3), the Court held, is an emergency measure, meant to operate strictly for as long as the non-compliance it responds to continues to threaten public health. Once an establishment demonstrates, through a proper re-inspection, that it has closed the gap, the suspension loses its statutory justification and ought to be lifted, subject only to an exceptional showing that some residual public health risk still remains. Treating a 97 per cent compliance score as insufficient to end a suspension imposed over a 69 per cent score, without identifying what specific risk survives, turns a protective measure into something closer to a punishment with no fixed term.

The bench was careful to separate that principle from the question of accountability for the original lapse. Nothing in the judgment lets an establishment off the hook for the conduct that triggered the suspension in the first place; the Court noted that distinct breaches, such as selling product categories not endorsed on the licence, or continuing to operate during a period when the suspension was validly in force, invite their own penal consequences under Sections 55 and 63 of the Act. Revoking the suspension once compliance is restored does not erase liability for violations that occurred before it was restored.

Its direction was that compliance, once properly verified, should translate into revocation of the suspension, coupled with continued monitoring as the regulatory framework already mandates, rather than a prolonged shutdown that serves no protective purpose. That monitoring obligation gives the authority a way to keep an eye on the establishment without using an indefinite suspension as the instrument for doing so.

For food businesses facing a Section 32(3) suspension anywhere in Maharashtra, the ruling gives a concrete benchmark: a credible re-inspection report showing substantial compliance shifts the burden onto the authority to justify, with specifics, why the suspension should continue at all. Authorities, for their part, will need to document any claimed residual risk carefully if they want to resist lifting a suspension once an establishment has demonstrably turned its compliance score around, rather than relying on the original violation alone to keep the shutters down indefinitely. The judgment also implicitly disciplines how appellate authorities under the Food Safety and Standards Act handle appeals against continued suspension. An appellate order that simply affirms the original suspension without engaging with an intervening re-inspection report leaves itself exposed exactly as the order against Hotel Alankar did. Appellate authorities reviewing such cases will now need to call for, and actually weigh, any re-inspection evidence placed before them, rather than treating the original violation as conclusive for as long as the licensing authority chooses not to revisit it. There is a wider point here for how emergency powers under food safety law get used across India, not just in Maharashtra. Section 32(3) exists because some risks to public health cannot wait for the ordinary cancellation process under Section 32's other sub-sections to run its course, but an emergency power that outlives the emergency it was meant to address starts to look like an ordinary penalty dressed up in urgent language. Courts elsewhere are likely to draw on this reasoning when FSSAI-linked suspensions are challenged on similar facts, where compliance has been restored but the licensing authority has simply let the suspension run on regardless.
why_it_matters: Food businesses facing a Section 32(3) FSSAI licence suspension now have High Court authority for the proposition that a strong re-inspection score should end the suspension, shifting the burden onto the licensing authority to identify any specific, ongoing public health risk if it wants to keep the suspension alive. The ruling does not shield an establishment from separate penalties for the original lapse or for operating in breach of a validly imposed suspension, but it stops authorities from treating suspension itself as an indefinite punishment.
card_summary: Bombay HC's Kolhapur Bench holds that an FSSAI licence suspension cannot continue once re-inspection shows the establishment has fixed the problem, rejecting its use as an open-ended penalty.
card_tip: After a Section 32(3) suspension, get a prompt re-inspection and use a strong score to press for revocation; absent a specific, ongoing risk, the authority cannot keep it running.
verification_notes: Confirmed via LiveLaw's report (dated 11 September 2026) describing the Bombay High Court Division Bench ruling that FSSAI licence suspension cannot continue infinitely, and Verdictum's case report citing 2026 BHC KOL 8650 (DB) with the same bench composition. Both sources corroborate the 7 July 2026 inspection and 69% score, the Section 32(3) suspension imposed 8 July 2026, the 31 July 2026 re-inspection recording 97% compliance, and the Court's distinction between lifting the suspension and separate liability under Sections 55 and 63 for breaches during the suspension period.
